snippet.title: If You Don't Know What a 'PIK' is, You Don't Know What's Quietly Breaking.
snippet.description:
This is rapidly spreading across private credit. Higher rates are squeezing borrowers to the point where the math stops working.

Now around 11.5% of these loans include PIK features. That’s up more than 72% since 2021.

And on paper, everything still looks fine. The loans are “performing.” Income is still reported. But no cash ever actually came in. PIKs blur that line, and most investors won’t notice until it's too late.

Earlier this year, Fitch recorded 11 default events in a single month. Nearly double the 2025 monthly average.

Of those defaults, 60% had one thing in common. They introduced PIKs first.

snippet.title: How SpaceX Is Making America Uncatchable
snippet.description:
SpaceX carries 90% of everything headed to orbit this year, but the spectacular rocket landing back on the pad is a distraction from what actually matters. For a thousand years, from Portuguese caravels to transcontinental railroads, the real wealth has never gone to the ones who left, it went to the ones who figured out how to come back.

The useful space around Earth is far smaller than it looks: a few narrow orbital bands, fewer than 1,900 slots in Geostationary Orbit, and one patch of ice at the Moon's south pole roughly the size of Switzerland. That ice is water, water is H2O, and the oxygen in it can be liquified into rocket fuel — whoever builds the first gas station on the Moon controls the only refueling point between here and Mars.

This video traces a pattern that keeps repeating: a new physical frontier opens, gatekeepers lose their grip, Maslow's hierarchy resets to the bottom layers, and selling picks and shovels becomes the most durable business on Earth. The same forces are now playing out in orbit, with Starlink, Amazon, Blue Origin, China, and others racing to fill the chokepoints before someone else does.

Whether that ends in generational wealth creation or a bubble rivaling the dot-com era depends on how fast rockets can close the physical gap between imagination and reality. A second video diving deeper into SpaceX's economics is coming in a few weeks.

localized.title: How SpaceX Is Making America Uncatchable
localized.description:
SpaceX carries 90% of everything headed to orbit this year, but the spectacular rocket landing back on the pad is a distraction from what actually matters. For a thousand years, from Portuguese caravels to transcontinental railroads, the real wealth has never gone to the ones who left, it went to the ones who figured out how to come back.

The useful space around Earth is far smaller than it looks: a few narrow orbital bands, fewer than 1,900 slots in Geostationary Orbit, and one patch of ice at the Moon's south pole roughly the size of Switzerland. That ice is water, water is H2O, and the oxygen in it can be liquified into rocket fuel — whoever builds the first gas station on the Moon controls the only refueling point between here and Mars.

This video traces a pattern that keeps repeating: a new physical frontier opens, gatekeepers lose their grip, Maslow's hierarchy resets to the bottom layers, and selling picks and shovels becomes the most durable business on Earth. The same forces are now playing out in orbit, with Starlink, Amazon, Blue Origin, China, and others racing to fill the chokepoints before someone else does.

Whether that ends in generational wealth creation or a bubble rivaling the dot-com era depends on how fast rockets can close the physical gap between imagination and reality. A second video diving deeper into SpaceX's economics is coming in a few weeks.

snippet.title: We think of black swans as unpredictable disasters. This was the other kind, the positive black swan
snippet.description:
1 in 5 deaths in WWII had nothing to do with bombs or bullets.

It was infection. A scraped knee, a chest cold, a routine surgery, any of them could kill you. Then a messy scientist left for vacation, a speck of mold drifted up through the floorboards from three floors down, and landed almost dead center in a petri dish he'd forgotten to clean.

The ring it left behind had wiped out every bacterium around it.

That one accident pulled death-from-infection from 1 in 5 down to less than 1 in 100. Hundreds of millions of lives saved, it made zero headlines.

Most black swans are catastrophes nobody saw coming. This was the rare one that broke the other way.

snippet.description:
One of the biggest misconceptions about interest rates is that they impact the economy immediately.

They don't.

When the Federal Reserve raises rates, the effects don't show up overnight. They ripple through the financial system slowly. If you want to understand where higher interest rates are really landing, you have to follow the money.

You have to look at who borrowed when money was cheap, who needs to refinance today, and who suddenly has to survive in a world where capital isn't free anymore.

And right now, there's one asset class that's starting to feel that pain more than anyone else.
